title: UNION ALL
description: Learn SQL UNION ALL with duplicate-preserving payment reports, column alignment, NULL rules, ordering, and worked aggregation exercises.

questions.question_text: What does UNION ALL do differently from plain UNION?
options: It keeps every row from both queries, including duplicates, with no de-duplication
It only returns rows common to both queries
It requires exactly matching column names
questions.explanation: UNION ALL skips the de-duplication step that plain UNION performs.

questions.question_text: If each of two source queries contributes student 2 exactly once, how often does student 2 appear under UNION ALL?
options: Twice — once from each source query, since UNION ALL doesn't deduplicate
questions.explanation: Without deduplication, a student present in both tables is counted from each source.

questions.question_text: When is UNION ALL the better choice over plain UNION?
options: When duplicates are impossible by construction, or when repeats should be preserved/counted rather than removed
Only when the two queries have different column counts
questions.explanation: Avoiding unnecessary de-duplication work is the direct performance benefit when duplicates aren't a concern.

questions.question_text: Does classic relational algebra (as covered in Chapter 7) have a direct equivalent to UNION ALL?
options: Yes, it's the primary form of Union in the algebra
No — classic relational algebra's Union assumes set (duplicate-free) semantics; UNION ALL is a SQL-specific bag-semantics extension
UNION ALL and relational Union are identical concepts
Relational algebra has no Union operation at all
questions.explanation: UNION ALL's duplicate-preserving nature doesn't map onto the classic set-based Union operation.

questions.question_text: What common mistake wastes performance unnecessarily?
options: Using UNION ALL when duplicates matter
Defaulting to plain UNION out of habit even when duplicates genuinely can't occur
Using ORDER BY with UNION ALL
questions.explanation: Unneeded de-duplication work is a real, avoidable cost when duplicates are already known to be impossible.

questions.question_text: If enrolled_2025 has 4 rows and enrolled_2026 has 3 rows, how many rows does UNION ALL return?
questions.explanation: UNION ALL simply concatenates both result sets without removing any rows.

questions.question_text: Do the column-count and type compatibility requirements (union-compatibility) still apply to UNION ALL?
options: No, only plain UNION has this requirement
Yes — the same union-compatibility rules apply to UNION ALL as to UNION
Only the type requirement applies, not column count
UNION ALL has no requirements at all
questions.explanation: Union-compatibility is a structural requirement independent of whether deduplication happens.

questions.question_text: Why is SQL described as having 'bag semantics' rather than pure set semantics?
options: SQL tables never contain duplicate rows
SQL tables and query results can contain duplicate rows by default, unlike the pure-set relations of classic relational algebra
Bag semantics only applies to UNION ALL, nowhere else in SQL
This is purely a theoretical distinction with no practical SQL consequence
questions.explanation: SQL's tolerance of duplicate rows throughout (not just in UNION ALL) is exactly what 'bag semantics' refers to.

questions.question_text: Two sources each contribute (500). What does UNION ALL return?
questions.explanation: UNION ALL retains multiplicity from both inputs.

questions.question_text: Why include a source label when combining local payment IDs?
options: To distinguish the same local ID in different systems
To force a primary key on the result
questions.explanation: A local identifier may only be unique within its source.

questions.question_text: Which branch determines the combined output column names?
options: The branch with an ORDER BY
questions.explanation: Output names are taken from the first query.

questions.question_text: What happens when one UNION ALL branch returns three columns and the other two?
questions.explanation: Each branch must provide the same column count.

questions.question_text: How are branch columns aligned?
questions.explanation: The first expression aligns with the first expression in every branch.

questions.question_text: Which clause guarantees order for the combined report?
options: The first table primary key alone
questions.explanation: Only explicit final ordering defines the requested result order.

questions.question_text: What is SUM after appending amounts 500, 500 and 800?
questions.explanation: All three occurrences contribute to the sum.

questions.question_text: Which count includes combined rows with NULL amounts?
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of nullable fields.

questions.question_text: What should be checked before appending mirrored event feeds?
options: Whether both tables have one row
Whether the query omits ORDER BY
Whether the same business events occur in both
questions.explanation: Overlapping event identities can cause double counting.

questions.question_text: Why can UNION ALL cost less than UNION?
options: It does not require duplicate elimination
questions.explanation: Avoiding duplicate elimination can save work, though other costs remain.

questions.question_text: What does an empty branch contribute?
questions.explanation: Appending an empty result adds no occurrences.

questions.question_text: Why explicitly cast a placeholder NULL?
options: To communicate a compatible intended type
questions.explanation: Casting clarifies the type contract for a missing source field.

coding_problems.title: Append All Payment Occurrences
coding_problems.task: Return channel, id, amount for every payment, with labels morning and evening. Order by channel, id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE morning (id INT PRIMARY KEY, amount INT); CREATE TABLE evening (id INT PRIMARY KEY, amount INT);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO morning VALUES (1,20),(2,20); INSERT INTO evening VALUES (1,20),(2,30);
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT 'morning' AS channel,id,amount FROM morning UNION ALL SELECT 'evening',id,amount FROM evening ORDER BY channel,id;
coding_problems.expected:
channel	id	amount
evening	1	20
evening	2	30
morning	1	20
morning	2	20

coding_problems.title: Total Appended Payments by Channel
coding_problems.task: Return channel, total for each nonempty source, preserving repeated amounts before aggregation. Order by channel.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE morning (id INT PRIMARY KEY, amount INT); CREATE TABLE evening (id INT PRIMARY KEY, amount INT);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO morning VALUES (1,20),(2,20); INSERT INTO evening VALUES (1,20),(2,30);
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT channel,SUM(amount) AS total FROM (SELECT 'morning' AS channel,amount FROM morning UNION ALL SELECT 'evening',amount FROM evening) AS p GROUP BY channel ORDER BY channel;

notes:
## Combining events without losing occurrences

A campus records payments from an online gateway and a finance desk. Both systems can record the amount 500 on the same day. A report must preserve both payments because equal amounts do not mean the same event. UNION ALL appends compatible query results while retaining every occurrence. Think of each input as a bag of rows: an output row appears as often as its inputs contribute it. This multiplicity is the central difference from UNION, which removes duplicate complete result rows.

Choose the result grain before selecting columns. If each row represents a payment, project payment identity, channel, amount, and date. If each row represents a distinct amount, deduplication might be intentional. Using UNION to repair an unexplained repeated payment can conceal a source ingestion bug. Using UNION ALL to merge overlapping copies of the same event can double a financial total. The operator preserves the rows supplied; it does not understand which events the business considers identical.

## Build a small reproducible example

Create two independent sources with local identifiers. The identifier 1 may exist in both systems without a conflict because its meaning includes the source. Decimal amounts avoid approximate arithmetic in this example. The nullable memo demonstrates that missing information can survive the combination.

```sql
CREATE TABLE web_payments (
 id INT PRIMARY KEY, amount DECIMAL(10,2), memo VARCHAR(30)
);
CREATE TABLE desk_payments (
 id INT PRIMARY KEY, amount DECIMAL(10,2), memo VARCHAR(30)
);
INSERT INTO web_payments VALUES (1,500.00,NULL),(2,500.00,'books');
INSERT INTO desk_payments VALUES (1,500.00,NULL),(2,800.00,'fees');
SELECT 'web' AS channel,id,amount,memo FROM web_payments
UNION ALL
SELECT 'desk',id,amount,memo FROM desk_payments
ORDER BY channel,id;
```

The expected rows are desk 1 with 500 and a missing memo, desk 2 with 800 and fees, web 1 with 500 and a missing memo, and web 2 with 500 and books. This is a reasoned example output, rather than a recorded execution result. The source label makes local identifiers unambiguous. Without that label, identical projected rows remain repeated under UNION ALL; they are still separate occurrences even when a display makes them look indistinguishable.

## Match columns by position

Each branch must return the same number of columns. SQL matches their positions, not their aliases. Selecting amount before id in one branch silently changes the meaning if compatible numeric types allow conversion. Treat every output position as a small contract: document its name, meaning, type, units, and nullability. A fee measured in cents is not interchangeable with a fee measured in currency units merely because both are integers.

The first query supplies the result column names. Later aliases do not rename the combined output. When a source lacks a field, an explicit typed NULL can communicate the intended shape. In MySQL, CAST(NULL AS CHAR(30)) is useful for an absent text memo. Compatible types are resolved across branches; exact conversion and collation rules are dialect dependent. Prefer explicit casts when combining dates, numeric text, or different string character sets, and test values that might be truncated or compared unexpectedly.

```sql
SELECT id,amount,memo FROM web_payments
UNION ALL
SELECT id,amount,CAST(NULL AS CHAR(30)) FROM desk_payments
ORDER BY id,amount;
```

This version deliberately discards desk memos. It is appropriate only if that projection matches the reporting requirement. Adding NULL just to make the column count match can produce a syntactically valid but misleading report. Projection decisions should follow the contract, rather than whichever columns happen to be easiest to combine.

## Duplicates, NULL, and counting

Consider projecting only amount from the sample. UNION ALL returns four occurrences: 500 three times and 800 once. UNION returns two distinct values. If both branches contain NULL amounts, UNION ALL retains every missing value, while duplicate elimination treats repeated NULL result rows as duplicates for the set operation. This does not change ordinary equality: NULL = NULL is still unknown in a WHERE predicate. Different SQL features use different comparison rules for their own purposes.

COUNT(*) on a combined derived table counts occurrences, including rows whose amount is NULL. COUNT(amount) ignores missing amounts. SUM(amount) ignores individual NULL amounts but returns NULL when there are no nonmissing input amounts. Use COALESCE only when the reporting definition says that a missing total should display as zero. A missing payment amount usually deserves investigation rather than silent conversion into a real zero payment.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS payments,SUM(amount) AS total
FROM (
 SELECT amount FROM web_payments
 UNION ALL
 SELECT amount FROM desk_payments
) AS p;
```

The sample contributes four payments totaling 2300.00. A novice substitution of UNION would produce 1300.00 because it removes repeated amounts before summation. This example shows why the columns used during duplicate elimination matter as much as the chosen operator. Including a distinct identifier changes which rows are considered duplicates.

## Ordering, limits, and filtering

The combined result has no promised order until a final ORDER BY specifies one. Do not assume the first branch is emitted before the second, even if a small experiment appears to behave that way. For pagination, include a stable tie breaker such as channel and id after the main sort field. Sorting by amount alone leaves the relative order of equal payments unspecified.

A filter inside a branch applies only to that source. A filter outside a derived union applies to every combined row. These can express the same requirement when the conditions and types match, but spelling out each branch filter often makes source specific conditions clearer. Branch limits and ordering require dialect appropriate parentheses and mean something different from a final limit. Selecting the top two rows from each source is not the same as selecting the top two rows overall.

## Worked lab: preserve source occurrences

The task is to list every payment above 400 with its channel and identifier. The solution adds a channel literal, applies the same threshold to both inputs, then orders the whole result by channel and id. All four sample rows qualify. Add another desk payment of 500: the output must grow by one. If it does not, inspect whether a distinct operation or grouping has accidentally removed an event.

A second lab asks for total revenue by channel. Combine labelled amounts in a derived table, group by channel, and sum within each group. The expected totals are desk 1300.00 and web 1000.00. An empty source contributes no rows; it does not automatically generate a channel with zero revenue. To show absent channels, start with a channel dimension and left join aggregated results. That is an additional reporting requirement, not a property of UNION ALL.

## A boundary case with mixed operations

When a longer statement mixes UNION and UNION ALL, do not infer duplicate behavior from just its first operator. Duplicate elimination can apply across a larger intermediate result according to the grouping and operator rules. Parenthesize the intended subexpressions and work through a tiny example containing the same value in every source. For maintainability, an explicit derived table followed by SELECT DISTINCT can communicate the final deduplication boundary more clearly. Preserve provenance until that boundary whenever investigators may need to explain where a row came from. Removing provenance early makes reconciliation harder even if the final totals happen to match today.

## Costs and practical checks

UNION ALL avoids the duplicate elimination work required by UNION, but it is not guaranteed to make every query faster. Branch scans, joins, sorting, network transfer, and final aggregation can dominate the cost. Inspect an execution plan and representative data before claiming a performance improvement. Returning unnecessary columns also increases memory and transfer work, even when no deduplication occurs.

Before shipping a combination, check source overlap, column alignment, types, nullable fields, and final ordering. Compare row counts with the sum of independently filtered source counts. Reconcile a few business identifiers across inputs when overlap is possible. Then test one empty input and two identical projected rows. These checks establish what the result means and help distinguish intentional repeated occurrences from accidental duplicate ingestion.

Continue with [Simple Views](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/simple-views) to give a reusable query a name, and revisit [UNION ALL](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/union-all) whenever a report must preserve source multiplicity.
